    AI Overview
    Petróleo (petroleum) is a fossil fuel formed from ancient organic matter, primarily plankton and algae, over millions of years. As a complex mixture of hydrocarbons, it is refined into essential fuels like gasoline and kerosene, as well as plastics and petrochemicals. It is extracted via drilling. 
    Key Details: 
    • Formation: It is not formed from dinosaurs, but from marine organic matter, primarily algae.
    • Geological Origin: Roughly 70% of oil deposits formed during the Mesozoic era.
    • Uses: Propels vehicles, heats buildings, produces electricity, and acts as a raw material for plastics.
    • Price Dynamics: As of April 17, 2026, crude oil prices fell to 83.85 USD/Bbl, marking a significant drop from late 2025 highs.
    • Major Entities: Petrobras is a prominent Brazilian state-owned company specializing in pre-salt oil exploration.

    About this result

    AI Overview
    Petroleum products are materials derived from crude oil refining, primarily categorized into transportation fuels (gasoline, diesel, jet fuel), heating oils, hydrocarbon gas liquids (propane, butane), lubricants, asphalt, and petrochemical feedstocks used to make plastics and chemicals. These products power vehicles, heat buildings, and provide materials for countless everyday items. 
    Main Types of Petroleum Products
    • Transportation Fuels:
      • Finished Motor Gasoline: The most consumed product, used in cars and light vehicles. 
      • Distillate Fuel Oil (Diesel Fuel): Used for heavy-duty vehicles, trucks, and trains. 
      • Jet Fuel: Used for aviation, including kerosene-type jet fuel. 
    • Heating and Fuel Oils:
      • Heating Oil: Used for residential and commercial heating. 
      • Residual Fuel Oils (No. 5, No. 6): Used for ships and industrial power generation. 
    • Hydrocarbon Gas Liquids (HGLs): Propane, butane, and ethane, which are used for heating, cooking, and petrochemical production. 
    • Petrochemical Feedstocks: Naphtha, ethane, and other gases that are raw materials for manufacturing plastics, synthetic fibers, rubber, and fertilizers. 
    • Lubricants: Motor oils, transmission fluids, and industrial lubricants. 
    • Asphalt and Road Oil: Used for road construction and waterproofing. 
    • Other Products: Kerosene, paraffin waxes, coke, and solvents. 
    Key Usage Breakdown (U.S. Data): 
    • Gasoline: ~44% of consumption.
    • Distillate Fuels: ~19% of consumption.
    • Hydrocarbon Gas Liquids: ~17% of consumption.
    • Jet Fuel: ~8% of consumption.

      Locations. Where is petroleum found?
      About this result

      An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
      AI Overview
      Petroleum (crude oil) is found in underground reservoirs trapped within sedimentary rock formations, both onshore and offshore, usually thousands of feet below the surface. Formed from ancient microscopic marine life, major deposits occur in porous rocks like sandstone or limestone sealed by impermeable rock layers, often located in the Middle East, North America (US, Canada), and offshore in the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico. 
      Key Locations of Petroleum Deposits:
      • Geological Settings:
        Petroleum collects in porous "reservoir" rocks—sandstone, limestone, or dolomite—trapped by layers of impermeable shale or clay. 
      • Major Global Regions:
        Nearly half of the world's proven reserves are in the Middle East. Other significant areas include North America (Canada and the U.S.), Latin America (Venezuela), Africa, and Russia. 
      • Offshore Locations:
        Significant oil deposits are found deep beneath the seabed, particularly in the "Golden Triangle" spanning the Gulf of Mexico, Brazil, and West Africa. 
      • Onshore Basins:
        Major on-land deposits exist in specific geologic formations, such as the Permian and Bakken formations in the U.S. 
      How It's Found:
      • Ancient Seas:
        Petroleum is formed over millions of years from the remains of microscopic marine organisms (plankton) that settled to the seafloor, covered by sediment, and subjected to immense heat and pressure. 
      • Traps:
        Because petroleum is less dense than water, it travels upwards through porous rocks until it hits an "impermeable" rock layer (a trap) that stops it from moving further, resulting in concentrated pools of oil and gas. 
      Top Oil-Producing Areas (Contextual):
      • United States: Key production occurs in Texas, New Mexico, North Dakota, Colorado, and Alaska. 
      • Canada: Features massive oil sands deposits in Alberta. 
      • Mexico: Known for major offshore fields like Cantarell.

        Formation. How is petroleum formed?
        Feedback
        Oil and gas are formed from organic material mainly deposited as sediments on the seabed and then broken down and transformed over millions of years. If there is a suitable combination of source rock, reservoir rock, cap rock and a trap in an area, recoverable oil and gas deposits may be discovered there.

        Environmental Impact. What is the environmental impact of petroleum?
        About this result
        Feedback
        An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
        AI Overview
        Petroleum has severe, wide-ranging environmental impacts across its lifecycle, including greenhouse gas emissions, habitat destruction from drilling, and water/soil contamination from spills. Burning petroleum products releases carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and toxic particles, causing air pollution, climate change, and acid rain. Oil spills destroy aquatic ecosystems, killing wildlife and polluting habitats. 
        Key environmental impacts include:
        • Climate Change & Air Quality:
          Burning gasoline and diesel releases carbon dioxide, a major greenhouse gas. Refining and combustion also release toxic pollutants like benzene and sulfur dioxide, contributing to smog and respiratory illnesses. 
        • Marine and Coastal Ecosystem Damage:
          Oil spills and drilling accidents devastate marine life, coating birds in oil, destroying coastal mangroves, and lowering oxygen levels in water. 
        • Land and Soil Degradation:
          Extraction activities, such as drilling and pipeline transportation, destroy wildlife habitats and degrade soil through spills and leaks. 
        • Water Contamination:
          Spills and leakage from extraction sites, including abandoned "orphan wells," contaminate groundwater and vital aquatic ecosystems. 
        • Health Consequences:
          Fossil fuel pollution contributes significantly to premature deaths from respiratory and cardiovascular diseases. 
        These impacts are often most severe near refining facilities and areas experiencing heavy transportation accidents.

          Chemical Composition. What is the chemical composition of petroleum?
          About this result
          Feedback
          An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
          AI Overview
          Petroleum is a complex liquid mixture composed primarily of hydrocarbons (90–95%), specifically carbon (
          82–87%82 – 87 %
          )           and hydrogen (
          11–15%11 – 15 %
          )          , formed from ancient organic matter.                     It mainly contains alkanes (paraffins), cycloalkanes (naphthenes), and aromatics, alongside small amounts of sulfur, nitrogen, oxygen, and trace metals like nickel and vanadium. 
          Key Elemental Composition: 
          • Carbon (
            Ccap C
            )            :
            83−87%83 minus 87 %
          • Hydrogen (
            Hcap H
            )            :
            11−16%11 minus 16 %
          • Sulfur (
            Scap S
            )            :
            0−4%0 minus 4 %
          • Nitrogen (
            Ncap N
            )            :
            0.1−2%0.1 minus 2 %
          • Oxygen (
            Ocap O
            )            :
            0.05−1.5%0.05 minus 1.5 %
          • Metals/Trace Elements:
            <0.1%is less than 0.1 %
            (Iron, Nickel, Vanadium, Copper)
          Major Hydrocarbon Classes: 
          1. Paraffins (Alkanes): Saturated straight or branched-chain hydrocarbons.
          2. Naphthenes (Cycloalkanes): Saturated ring compounds.
          3. Aromatics: Unsaturated ring-type compounds, including benzene.
          4. Asphaltics: Heavy, complex mixtures.
          The exact composition varies depending on the oil field, but the elemental percentages remain relatively consistent.
